standards_gaps.gap: Voluntary, non-prescriptive framework: the four functions (Govern/Map/Measure/Manage) organize trustworthiness considerations but set no technical threshold, conformance test, or required red-team method — operationalization is deferred to the companion Playbook and to the Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) ^[inferred]

ISMS controls (Annex A 2022) govern information security management generically; they predate and do not address AI-specific adversarial threats (model extraction, training-data poisoning, prompt injection) — an AI system inherits ISMS coverage only for its conventional IT surface ^[inferred]

PIMS extension to 27001/27002 covers privacy information management but has no provisions for inference-time privacy leakage, membership-inference, or training-data memorization specific to ML models ^[inferred]

TR 24029-1 assesses neural-network robustness via statistical methods (formal/empirical) but is a technical report (non-normative) scoped to robustness measurement — it sets no adversarial-attack test suite and does not cover generative/LLM jailbreak robustness ^[inferred]

Software-lifecycle process standard (ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207:2017) defines generic SDLC processes but has no AI/ML-specific lifecycle activities (data engineering, model training/validation, red-team gates, continuous post-deployment evaluation) — agentic-SDLC assurance falls outside its process model ^[inferred]

Software-testing standard series (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119 parts 1-5) defines test processes, documentation, and techniques for deterministic software — it has no constructs for non-deterministic/probabilistic model testing, metamorphic testing of ML, or adversarial/red-team test design for LLMs ^[inferred]

Vulnerability-disclosure standard defines how vendors receive and disclose vulnerability information for conventional software/hardware; it has no AI-specific disclosure schema (model flaws, jailbreak classes, data-poisoning, evals) and no coordination model for shared frontier-model risk — the CVD/VDP-for-AI gap ^[inferred]

Vulnerability-handling-process standard defines internal triage/remediation workflow; it presumes a patchable software artifact and does not model the AI case where a 'fix' is a guardrail/retrain/eval-gate and where the same model weights are shared across many deployers ^[inferred]

Community awareness list (not a normative/certifiable standard): enumerates the top LLM-application risk classes (LLM01 Prompt Injection ... LLM10) but provides no conformance test, severity threshold, or assurance methodology — it is a checklist, not an auditable control set ^[inferred]

Web-application security awareness list (A01-A10); generic to web apps and not specific to AI/LLM systems — referenced as the baseline secure-coding lens for AI-generated code, but provides no AI-specific coverage ^[inferred]

standards_gaps.ref: OWASP Agentic AI Threats and Mitigations
standards_gaps.gap: Threat-and-mitigation guidance (OWASP GenAI Security Project, Agentic AI Top 15) for autonomous-agent systems; valuable threat enumeration but non-normative, no conformance test, and overlaps the standards void for agentic/MCP/A2A assurance ^[inferred]

Web Security Testing Guide is a methodology for manual/automated web-app penetration testing; no coverage of model/LLM testing, adversarial prompt testing, or agentic-system test methodology ^[inferred]

Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems is a living knowledge base of adversary tactics/techniques (ATT&CK-style) for ML — descriptive, not a conformance standard; it catalogues TTPs but defines no required defensive controls or assurance test ^[inferred]
Enterprise adversary-behavior knowledge base for conventional cyber operations; the AI-specific extension lives in ATLAS, so ATT&CK alone leaves model/LLM-layer techniques uncovered ^[inferred]

Adversarial Machine Learning taxonomy/terminology report: authoritative classification of attacks (evasion, poisoning, privacy, abuse) and mitigations across predictive and generative AI — but a taxonomy report, not a conformance standard; it names attack classes without prescribing tested defenses ^[inferred]

General Data Protection Regulation governs personal-data processing and automated decision-making (Art. 22) but predates generative AI: no provisions for training-data memorization, model-inversion privacy leakage, or LLM output containing personal data — applied to AI by interpretation rather than AI-specific rule ^[inferred]

standards_gaps.ref: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI
standards_gaps.gap: Soft-law ethics recommendation (193 member-state instrument) sets values/principles (human rights, transparency, accountability) and a Readiness Assessment Methodology — non-binding, no conformance test or technical control; an aspirational governance frame rather than an assurance standard ^[inferred]

standards_gaps.ref: EU HLEG Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI
standards_gaps.gap: High-Level Expert Group guidelines define seven requirements for Trustworthy AI plus the ALTAI self-assessment checklist — influential precursor to the EU AI Act but itself non-binding self-assessment, no conformance test or red-team requirement ^[inferred]

AILuminate is a benchmark/grading suite (12 hazard categories, 5-grade safety scale) from the MLCommons AI Risk & Reliability working group — a de facto evaluation methodology, not a formal standard; benchmark contamination, narrow hazard coverage, and lack of formal conformance limit assurance value ^[inferred]

Responsible Scaling Policy is a single-vendor governance commitment (AI Safety Levels / capability thresholds gating deployment) — voluntary, self-defined, self-enforced; not interoperable, auditable, or a multi-party standard. Represents the frontier-lab-policy class the standards landscape has not yet codified ^[inferred]

Voluntary commitments by leading AI companies (safety, security, trust — incl. red-team testing and info-sharing) brokered by the White House (2023) — non-binding pledges, no conformance mechanism or enforcement; a policy precursor rather than a standard ^[inferred]

Frontier AI Safety Commitments (Seoul AI Summit, May 2024): 16 signatory companies pledge to publish safety frameworks with capability thresholds and to not deploy past unmitigated severe risk — voluntary, self-defined thresholds, no independent verification or conformance test ^[inferred]

Under development: guidance on addressing security threats and failures in AI systems — intended to fill the AI-security void between ISMS (27001) and AI management (42001), but not yet published, so no normative coverage is available today ^[ambiguous]

Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF v1.1) defines secure-SDLC practices for conventional software; the AI-specific companion SP 800-218A (Secure Software Development Practices for Generative AI and Dual-Use Foundation Models) extends it to model development — but 800-218 itself has no AI-specific practice ^[inferred]

AIMS is process/management-level: Annex A controls (e.g. A.6 AI system lifecycle) require red teaming and risk treatment but specify no technical method, threshold, or conformance test for adversarial robustness — leaves agentic/runtime threats to organizational discretion ^[inferred]

Guidance (non-certifiable) adapts ISO 31000 to AI risk sources but predates agentic/tool-use and MCP/A2A threat classes — its risk-source annex has no entries for autonomous tool invocation, multi-agent coordination, or long-horizon attack ^[inferred]

Technical Report (informative only, not normative): describes properties/methods for combining AI with functional safety across three scenarios but cannot be certified against — the normative successor ISO/IEC TS 22440 is still in committee draft

First normative AI functional-safety spec still at Committee Draft (CD) stage (Part 1 Requirements, Part 2 Guidance) as of 2026 — no published normative AI functional-safety requirement exists; safety-critical autonomous-driving/medical/ICS deployments lack a certifiable AI-specific functional-safety baseline in the interim ^[inferred]

AI system impact-assessment guidance (non-certifiable, no external auditor) addresses societal/individual harm assessment but does not prescribe adversarial-testing or red-team evidence as an impact-assessment input — impact assessment and red-team findings remain unlinked ^[inferred]

Specifies competence/audit-time requirements for bodies certifying AIMS against 42001 but defines no auditor competence in adversarial ML / red teaming — AIMS certification can be granted without red-team capability assessment ^[inferred]

Software-lifecycle classes A/B/C and ISO 14971 linkage predate ML/AI-as-medical-device: no normative treatment of training-data provenance, model drift, continuous learning, or adversarial robustness for SaMD ^[inferred]

The Threat→Hazard→Hazardous-Situation→Harm→Risk→Control chain is med-device-specific; reused for AI harm modeling but has no AI-native hazard categories (jailbreak, prompt injection, agent goal-misalignment) — mapping to AI threats is analyst-supplied, not normative ^[inferred]

standards_gaps.ref: NIST AI 600-1 (Generative AI Profile) + AI RMF 1.0
standards_gaps.gap: Voluntary framework: 12 GenAI risk areas and 200+ suggested actions (GOVERN/MAP/MEASURE/MANAGE) are non-binding and method-agnostic — no required red-team protocol, no agentic-AI risk area, no MCP/A2A coverage; CBRN coverage is informational uplift only ^[inferred]

standards_gaps.ref: EU AI Act Art. 73 (serious-incident reporting) + Art. 55(1)(c) GPAI
standards_gaps.gap: Binding incident-reporting law, but Art. 73 obligations for high-risk systems apply only from 2 Aug 2026 and the 'serious incident' definition is outcome-based (death, critical-infrastructure disruption, fundamental-rights infringement) — pre-harm red-team flaw discovery, near-misses, and most agentic jailbreaks fall outside the mandatory-report trigger ^[inferred]

standards_gaps.ref: NIST CAISI (Center for AI Standards and Innovation, ex-US AISI)
standards_gaps.gap: Conducts pre-deployment frontier evals via voluntary developer agreements but produces no public normative standard or required conformance method — evaluation methodology is non-public and non-binding; 2025 rename from 'Safety Institute' narrowed scope to demonstrable cyber/bio/chem national-security risks, deprioritizing alignment/societal harm ^[inferred]

standards_gaps.ref: UK AISI Inspect / Inspect Evals (de facto eval harness)
standards_gaps.gap: Inspect is an open-source evaluation framework and a de facto standard harness for dangerous-capability/safeguard evals (AgentHarm, CyberSecEval), but no SDO has adopted it or any eval harness as a normative conformance method — frontier-eval methodology remains institute-specific and unstandardized across US CAISI / UK AISI / J-AISI ^[inferred]

No published normative standard addresses tool-calling agent assurance: AgentHarm/AgentDojo show leading agents complete malicious multi-step tasks and are broken by prompt injection over untrusted tool data, yet no ISO/IEC, NIST, or EU instrument specifies controls (tool allowlisting, capability scoping, HITL gates) or a conformance test for agentic robustness — 42001 Annex A and NIST AI RMF stop at GenAI, not agents ^[inferred]

Emerging agent-communication protocols (MCP, A2A, Agora, ANP) carry protocol-level trust risks — missing validation of executable components, no agent identity attestation, weak inter-agent authorization — and no SDO standard governs agent identity, capability delegation, or trust establishment across them; protocols are vendor-driven specs, not normative standards ^[inferred]

Standards treat red teaming as a point-in-time pre-deployment activity (42001 lifecycle, NIST RMF MEASURE, J-AISI methodology). Microsoft's 100-product lessons and the agentic threat surface argue red teaming must be continuous/runtime against deployed, drifting, tool-using systems — but no normative standard specifies continuous-red-teaming cadence, runtime-monitoring evidence, or re-certification triggers on model/behavior change ^[inferred]

standards_gaps.ref: GAP: Coordinated AI flaw disclosure (CVD/VDP for AI)
standards_gaps.gap: Infosec CVD/VDP (CVE/CWE, bug bounties, safe harbor, bounded remediation windows) does not yet extend cleanly to AI: no AI-flaw identifier scheme (no 'AI-CVE'), no standardized flaw-report schema, no normalized safe-harbor for AI red-teamers, and no multi-party coordination protocol for jailbreaks that affect many models/vendors at once. Existing channels (AIID, OECD AIM, EU Art. 73, ATLAS case studies) are siloed and non-interoperable; agentic systems strain CVD further (dynamic behavior, multi-party tool chains, emergent harms) ^[inferred]

LLM-as-judge evaluators (used to score ASR in HarmBench, JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT, AgentHarm, and the BFSI ensemble-judge RAHS) are the load-bearing measurement instrument of AI red teaming, yet no standard defines validity, inter-rater calibration against human ground truth, bias/gaming resistance, or a conformance test for a judge — StrongREJECT itself shows judge choice swings reported attack success, so unstandardized judges make cross-benchmark numbers non-comparable ^[inferred]

Sector evidence (healthcare clinician-in-loop, BFSI risk-adjusted harm scoring, legal RAG 17-33% hallucination, automotive CARLA adversarial driving, child-safety AIG-CSAM, defense DARPA SABER) shows the SAME technique has a different harm profile and verification protocol per domain, yet horizontal standards (42001, NIST RMF, J-AISI methodology) are sector-agnostic and no sectoral AI-red-teaming conformance profiles exist except partial med-device (IEC 62304/ISO 14971) and emerging defense T&E ^[inferred]

standards_candidates.candidate: Standard candidate: a measurable conformance/assurance profile that turns AI RMF Measure-function outcomes into testable adversarial-robustness criteria (SC 42 / NIST cross-walk)
Standard candidate: an AI-security control extension to Annex A (aligns with the in-development ISO/IEC 27090 AI-security guidance)
Standard candidate: extend the 24029 robustness-assessment series to adversarial/jailbreak robustness for generative models (SC 42 WG3)
Standard candidate: an AI/agentic-SDLC process profile layering ML data/model/red-team activities onto 12207 (bridges to ISO/IEC 5338 AI system lifecycle)
Standard candidate: an AI-testing part of the 29119 family covering probabilistic, metamorphic, and adversarial test design (SC 42 / SC 7 liaison)
Standard candidate: an AI-flaw disclosure profile extending 29147 (taxonomy + schema for model vulnerabilities; aligns with std-gap-cvd-vdp-ai-disclosure)
Standard candidate: AI vulnerability-handling process profile (model-weight remediation, guardrail/eval-gate as fix, multi-deployer coordination) extending 30111
Standard candidate: map OWASP LLM Top 10 risk classes to certifiable controls in an AI-security standard (ISO/IEC 27090 / 42001 Annex extension)

standards_candidates.ref: OWASP Agentic AI Threats and Mitigations
standards_candidates.candidate: Standard candidate: certifiable agentic-AI security controls (tool-use mediation, agent identity, multi-agent trust) — aligns with std-gap-agentic-tool-use and std-gap-mcp-a2a-trust
Standard candidate: bind ATLAS technique IDs to required controls in a certifiable AI-security standard (control-coverage conformance against ATLAS matrix)
Standard candidate: turn the NIST AML taxonomy into a testable control/eval matrix (mitigation conformance per attack class)
Standard candidate: elevate a benchmark-governance methodology (contamination control, hazard-taxonomy coverage, grading validity) into a normative AI-safety-evaluation standard (SC 42)
Standard candidate: a cross-vendor frontier-safety-policy standard (interoperable capability thresholds, eval gates, independent audit) generalizing RSP/FSF commitments
Standard candidate: an auditable conformance scheme for the Seoul Frontier Safety Commitments (threshold disclosure + third-party verification) — pairs with std-anthropic-rsp candidate
Standard candidate (new-discovery): track and accelerate ISO/IEC 27090 as the certifiable AI-security control standard the corpus repeatedly gestures at (27001/OWASP-LLM/ATLAS gaps)
Standard candidate (new-discovery): adopt SP 800-218A generative-AI secure-development practices as the SDLC assurance baseline for agentic/code-gen threats
Standard candidate: AI/ML extension or amendment to IEC 62304 covering data-driven SaMD lifecycle (training-data governance, model-update/PCCP integration, adversarial-robustness verification)

standards_candidates.ref: EU AI Act Art. 73 (serious-incident reporting) + Art. 55(1)(c) GPAI
standards_candidates.candidate: Standard candidate: harmonized EU AI-incident taxonomy + machine-readable serious-incident report schema interoperable with OECD AIM and AI Incident Database, extending Art. 73 reporting to near-miss/red-team flaw classes

standards_candidates.ref: UK AISI Inspect / Inspect Evals (de facto eval harness)
standards_candidates.candidate: Standard candidate: interoperable AI-evaluation harness conformance profile + shared dangerous-capability eval reporting schema for cross-institute (CAISI/AISI/J-AISI) comparability and result portability

Standard candidate: AI agent assurance profile — normative controls + conformance test method for tool-invocation gating, capability scoping, planning-risk bounds, and prompt-injection robustness in tool-using agents (extends ISO/IEC 42001 Annex A)

Standard candidate: A2A/MCP agent identity-attestation & trust-establishment profile — verifiable agent identity, scoped capability delegation tokens, executable-component validation, and cross-protocol authorization semantics

Standard candidate: Continuous & runtime AI red-teaming conformance profile — defines cadence, runtime-monitoring evidence requirements, drift/behavior-change re-certification triggers, and links runtime red-team findings to AIMS (42001) corrective-action and incident-reporting (EU AI Act Art. 73) pathways

standards_candidates.ref: GAP: Coordinated AI flaw disclosure (CVD/VDP for AI)
standards_candidates.candidate: Standard candidate: Coordinated AI flaw-disclosure reporting schema + multi-party AI vulnerability coordination protocol — AI-flaw identifier scheme (AI-CVE/CWE analogue), machine-readable standardized flaw report, safe-harbor/authorization template (per disclose.io) for AI red-teamers, severity rubric (CVSS adaptation + harm-based), embargo/coordination timeline, and a Disclosure Coordination Center routing findings to AIID/OECD-AIM/EU-AI-Office/vendors

Standard candidate: Conformance test method for LLM-as-judge evaluators — defines required human-agreement calibration, reliability/inter-rater metrics, adversarial-robustness of the judge, reporting of judge provenance, and a validity profile so attack-success-rate numbers are comparable across benchmarks and institutes

Standard candidate: family of sector AI-red-teaming verification profiles (medical, financial, legal, automotive, child-safety, defense) layering domain harm taxonomies, domain-expert-in-the-loop requirements, and sector-calibrated severity scoring onto a horizontal red-team baseline (e.g. J-AISI methodology)
